narrative:
The model predicted a 56% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest influence, both pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Being ranked in the bottom decile in both years—one compared to an average of about 6 among accepted students—signaled consistent academic struggle relative to your peers. This was the dominant reason the model doubted your likelihood of passing the bar.

Your LSAT score of 40 was the second most important factor. This score actually worked in your favor, pulling the prediction slightly toward passing. It sits above the average of 37 among accepted students, showing solid aptitude on the exam.

Your first-year ranking again appeared as the third most influential element, reinforcing the concern about your academic performance.

Taken together, the model saw your unusually low class standings as outweighing the positive signal from your LSAT, resulting in the rejection.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening your academic record. Consider retaking key courses, enrolling in a post-baccalaureate program, or gaining structured study support to raise your performance to the level of successful applicants. Improving those class rankings will have the biggest impact on future predictions. (248 words)
